problem: Let $a_1, a_2, a_3, \ldots$ be an infinite sequence of positive integers greater than $1$. Suppose that for all positive integers $n$, the number $a_{n+1}$ is the smallest positive integer greater than $a_n$ such that $\operatorname{gcd}(a_{n+1}, a_i) > 1$ for every $i = 1,2,\ldots,n$. Prove that there exist positive integers $T$ and $L$ such that $$a_{n+T} = a_n + L$$ for every positive integer $n$. (Note that $\operatorname{gcd}(x,y)$ denotes the greatest common divisor of positive integers $x$ and $y$.)
proof:
### 1. The set \(V\) and its relation to the sequence

Define  
\[
V = \{\, x \in \mathbb{N} \mid x > 1 \text{ and } \gcd(x, a_i) > 1 \text{ for all } i \ge 1 \,\}.
\]

**Lemma 1.** For every \(n \ge 1\),
\[
a_{n+1} = \min\{\, x \in V \mid x > a_n \,\}.
\]

*Proof.* By definition, \(a_{n+1}\) is the smallest integer \(> a_n\) such that \(\gcd(a_{n+1}, a_i) > 1\) for all \(i = 1,\dots,n\). Hence \(a_{n+1}\) satisfies the condition for the first \(n\) terms. We show that in fact \(\gcd(a_{n+1}, a_i) > 1\) for all \(i \ge 1\), i.e., \(a_{n+1} \in V\). For \(i \le n+1\) this holds by construction (for \(i=n+1\), \(\gcd(a_{n+1}, a_{n+1}) = a_{n+1} > 1\)). For any \(i > n+1\), when \(a_i\) was chosen it had to satisfy \(\gcd(a_i, a_j) > 1\) for all \(j < i\); in particular \(\gcd(a_i, a_{n+1}) > 1\). Thus \(\gcd(a_{n+1}, a_i) > 1\) for all \(i\). Therefore \(a_{n+1} \in V\).

Conversely, if \(x \in V\) and \(x > a_n\), then \(\gcd(x, a_i) > 1\) for all \(i \le n\), so \(x\) is a valid candidate for \(a_{n+1}\). By minimality of \(a_{n+1}\), we have \(a_{n+1} \le x\). Hence \(a_{n+1}\) is exactly the smallest element of \(V\) greater than \(a_n\). ∎

**Corollary 1.** \(a_1 \in V\) and the sequence \((a_n)_{n\ge 1}\) is exactly the increasing enumeration of \(V \cap [a_1, \infty)\).

*Proof.* For any \(i \ge 2\), when \(a_i\) is chosen we must have \(\gcd(a_i, a_1) > 1\) because \(1 \le i-1\). Also \(\gcd(a_1, a_1) = a_1 > 1\). Hence \(a_1 \in V\).

By Lemma 1, \(a_{n+1}\) is the smallest element of \(V\) greater than \(a_n\). Starting from \(a_1\), the sequence lists elements of \(V\) in strictly increasing order. We must show that every element of \(V\) that is \(\ge a_1\) appears in the sequence. Let \(y \in V\) with \(y \ge a_1\). Since \((a_n)\) is strictly increasing and infinite, it tends to infinity. The set \(\{n \mid a_n \le y\}\) is non‑empty (it contains \(1\) because \(a_1 \le y\)) and bounded above, so it has a maximum element \(n\). If \(a_n = y\), then \(y\) is in the sequence. If \(a_n < y\), then by maximality of \(n\) we have \(y < a_{n+1}\). But \(a_{n+1}\) is the smallest element of \(V\) greater than \(a_n\), and \(y \in V\) with \(y > a_n\), so we must have \(a_{n+1} \le y\), a contradiction. Therefore \(a_n = y\), and \(y\) appears in the sequence. Thus \((a_n)\) enumerates all of \(V \cap [a_1, \infty)\) in increasing order. ∎

### 2. Minimal elements of \(V\)

Let \(M\) be the set of minimal elements of \(V\) with respect to divisibility:
\[
M = \{\, m \in V \mid \text{no proper divisor } d > 1 \text{ of } m \text{ belongs to } V \,\}.
\]
(Since \(V \neq \emptyset\), we can pick any \(m \in V\) and consider the set of divisors \(d > 1\) of \(m\) that belong to \(V\). This set is finite and non‑empty (it contains \(m\)). Choosing an element minimal with respect to divisibility yields a minimal element of \(V\). Thus \(M\) is non‑empty.)

**Lemma 2.** Every \(m \in M\) is squarefree.

*Proof.* Suppose \(p^2 \mid m\) for some prime \(p\). Then \(m/p\) has the same prime factors as \(m\). For any \(i \ge 1\), since \(\gcd(m, a_i) > 1\), there is a prime \(q\) dividing both \(m\) and \(a_i\). If \(q = p\), then \(p^2 \mid m\) implies \(p \mid m/p\); if \(q \neq p\), then \(q \mid m/p\) trivially. In either case \(q \mid m/p\), so \(\gcd(m/p, a_i) \ge q > 1\). Thus \(m/p \in V\), contradicting the minimality of \(m\). ∎

**Corollary 2.** \(V = \{\, x > 1 \mid \exists\, m \in M,\; m \mid x \,\}\).

*Proof.* If \(x \in V\), consider the set of divisors \(d > 1\) of \(x\) that belong to \(V\). This set is non‑empty (it contains \(x\)) and finite. Choose a divisor \(m\) that is minimal with respect to divisibility. Then \(m \in M\) and \(m \mid x\). Conversely, if \(m \in M\) and \(m \mid x\), then for every \(i \ge 1\), \(\gcd(x, a_i) \ge \gcd(m, a_i) > 1\), so \(x \in V\). ∎

### 3. Auxiliary sets \(V_k\) and witnesses

For \(k \ge 1\) define
\[
V_k = \{\, x > 1 \mid \gcd(x, a_i) > 1 \text{ for } i = 1,\dots,k \,\},
\]
and set \(V_0 = \{ x > 1 \}\). Note that \(V_1 \supseteq V_2 \supseteq \cdots\) and \(V = \bigcap_{k\ge 1} V_k\). For \(K \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}\) we write \(V_{K-1}\) with the understanding that \(V_\infty = V\). We will only consider minimal elements of \(V_{K-1}\) with \(K \ge 2\) (so that \(K-1 \ge 1\)).

Let \(x\) be a minimal element of \(V_{K-1}\) (with respect to divisibility). For each prime \(p \mid x\) define
\[
j(x,p) = \min\{\, n \ge 1 \mid \gcd(x/p, a_n) = 1 \,\}.
\]
This minimum exists because \(x/p \notin V_{K-1}\): if \(x/p > 1\) this follows from the minimality of \(x\); if \(x/p = 1\) then \(1 \notin V_{K-1}\) (since \(V_{K-1}\) contains only numbers \(>1\)). In the case \(K < \infty\) we also have \(j(x,p) \le K-1\), because if \(\gcd(x/p, a_n) > 1\) for all \(n \le K-1\) then \(x/p\) would belong to \(V_{K-1}\), contradicting \(x/p \notin V_{K-1}\).

Define
\[
i(x) = \max_{p\mid x} j(x,p),
\]
and let \(p(x)\) be the smallest prime achieving this maximum.

**Properties of \(x\) (with \(i = i(x)\), \(p = p(x)\)):**

**Property 0.** If \(K < \infty\) then \(i(x) \le K-1\). (Immediate from \(j(x,p) \le K-1\) for all \(p\).)

**Property 1.** \(i = j(x,p)\). (By definition of \(p\).)

**Property 2.** \(p \mid a_i\).  
*Proof.* Since \(x \in V_{K-1}\), we have \(\gcd(x, a_i) > 1\). (If \(K < \infty\), this follows from \(i \le K-1\) by Property 0; if \(K = \infty\), it follows from \(x \in V\).) By definition of \(j(x,p)=i\), we have \(\gcd(x/p, a_i) = 1\). If \(p \nmid a_i\), then \(\gcd(x, a_i) = \gcd(x/p, a_i) = 1\), a contradiction. Hence \(p \mid a_i\). ∎

**Property 3.** For any \(q \mid x\), \(q \neq p\), we have \(j(x,q) < i\).  
*Proof.* Since \(p \mid a_i\) (Property 2) and \(p \mid x/q\) (because \(q \neq p\)), we have \(\gcd(x/q, a_i) \ge p > 1\). Thus the smallest index \(n\) with \(\gcd(x/q, a_n)=1\) cannot be \(i\). Since \(j(x,q) \le i\) (because \(i\) is the maximum), we must have \(j(x,q) < i\). ∎

**Property 4.** No other prime factor of \(x\) divides \(a_i\).  
*Proof.* If \(q \mid x\), \(q \neq p\), and \(q \mid a_i\), then \(q \mid x/p\), so \(\gcd(x/p, a_i) \ge q > 1\), contradicting \(\gcd(x/p, a_i)=1\). ∎

**Property 5.** If \(i \ge 2\), then \(x/p \in V_{i-1}\) and \(x/p > 1\).  
*Proof.* For \(n < i\), since \(j(x,p)=i\), we have \(\gcd(x/p, a_n) > 1\). Thus \(x/p \in V_{i-1}\). If \(x/p = 1\), then \(x = p\), so \(j(x,p)=1\), contradicting \(i \ge 2\). Hence \(x/p > 1\). ∎

**Property 6.** If \(i \ge 2\), then \(x \in V_i\).  
*Proof.* For \(n < i\), since \(x/p \in V_{i-1}\) (Property 5), we have \(\gcd(x/p, a_n) > 1\), so \(\gcd(x, a_n) > 1\). For \(n = i\), since \(p \mid a_i\) (Property 2) and \(p \mid x\), we have \(\gcd(x, a_i) \ge p > 1\). Thus \(\gcd(x, a_n) > 1\) for all \(n \le i\), so \(x \in V_i\). ∎

**Property 7.** \(x\) is squarefree.  
*Proof.* Suppose \(p^2 \mid x\) for some prime \(p\). Then \(x/p\) has the same prime factors as \(x\). For any \(n\) with \(1 \le n \le K-1\) (if \(K < \infty\)) or all \(n \ge 1\) (if \(K = \infty\)), since \(x \in V_{K-1}\), we have \(\gcd(x, a_n) > 1\). Let \(q\) be a common prime divisor. Then \(q \mid x/p\) (if \(q = p\), then \(p^2 \mid x\) implies \(p \mid x/p\); if \(q \neq p\), then \(q \mid x/p\) trivially). Hence \(\gcd(x/p, a_n) \ge q > 1\). Therefore \(x/p \in V_{K-1}\), contradicting the minimality of \(x\). ∎

### 4. Elements with witness 1

**Lemma 4.** Let \(x\) be a minimal element of \(V_{K-1}\) with \(K \ge 2\). If \(i(x) = 1\), then \(x\) is a prime dividing \(a_1\).

*Proof.* Since \(i(x)=1\), for every prime \(p \mid x\) we have \(j(x,p)=1\), i.e., \(\gcd(x/p, a_1)=1\). Suppose \(x\) has at least two distinct prime factors \(p\) and \(q\). Then \(x/p\) is divisible by \(q\), so \(\gcd(x/p, a_1)=1\) implies \(q \nmid a_1\). Similarly, \(x/q\) is divisible by \(p\), so \(p \nmid a_1\). For any other prime factor \(r\) of \(x\), pairing with \(p\) shows \(r \nmid a_1\). Thus no prime factor of \(x\) divides \(a_1\), so \(\gcd(x, a_1)=1\). But \(x \in V_{K-1}\) and \(K-1 \ge 1\), so \(\gcd(x, a_1) > 1\), contradiction. Hence \(x\) has exactly one distinct prime factor. By Property 7, \(x\) is squarefree, so \(x = p\) is prime. Then \(\gcd(p, a_1) > 1\) implies \(p \mid a_1\). ∎

### 5. Finiteness of minimal elements of \(V_{i-1}\)

**Lemma 5.** For any \(i \ge 2\), the set of minimal elements of \(V_{i-1}\) (with respect to divisibility) is finite.

*Proof.* Let \(y\) be a minimal element of \(V_{i-1}\). Then \(y > 1\) and \(\gcd(y, a_j) > 1\) for all \(j = 1,\dots,i-1\).

*Squarefreeness.* If \(p^2 \mid y\), then \(y/p\) has the same prime factors as \(y\). For each \(j \le i-1\), any common prime factor of \(y\) and \(a_j\) divides \(y/p\) (if it is \(p\), then \(p^2 \mid y\) implies \(p \mid y/p\); otherwise it divides \(y/p\) directly). Hence \(\gcd(y/p, a_j) \ge \gcd(y, a_j) > 1\). Thus \(y/p \in V_{i-1}\), contradicting minimality. So \(y\) is squarefree.

*Prime factors.* Every prime factor \(q\) of \(y\) must divide at least one of \(a_1,\dots,a_{i-1}\). Suppose \(q \mid y\) but \(q \nmid a_j\) for all \(j \le i-1\). If \(y = q\), then \(\gcd(q, a_j) = 1\) for all \(j\), contradiction. If \(y > q\), then \(y/q > 1\). For each \(j\), since \(q \nmid a_j\), any common divisor of \(y\) and \(a_j\) cannot include \(q\), so it divides \(y/q\). Therefore \(\gcd(y/q, a_j) = \gcd(y, a_j) > 1\). Thus \(y/q \in V_{i-1}\), contradicting minimality. Hence all prime factors of \(y\) belong to the finite set \(\bigcup_{j=1}^{i-1} \mathcal{P}(a_j)\), where \(\mathcal{P}(a_j)\) denotes the set of prime divisors of \(a_j\).

Since \(y\) is squarefree, it is a product of a subset of this finite set. There are only finitely many such products. Hence the set of minimal elements of \(V_{i-1}\) is finite. ∎

### 6. Key Lemma

**Lemma 6 (Key Lemma).** Let \(i \ge 2\). Let \(S\) be an infinite set of squarefree integers \(>1\) such that for each \(x \in S\):
(a) \(x\) is a minimal element of some \(V_{K_x-1}\) (\(K_x \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}\)) and \(x \in V_i\);
(b) there is a fixed prime \(p\) with \(p \mid x\) for all \(x \in S\);
(c) \(j(x,p) = i\) for all \(x \in S\);
(d) for all \(q \mid x\) with \(q \neq p\) we have \(j(x,q) < i\).
Then a contradiction arises.

*Proof.* For each \(x \in S\), since \(j(x,p)=i\), we have \(\gcd(x/p, a_i) = 1\). Also \(x \in V_i\) implies \(\gcd(x, a_j) > 1\) for all \(j \le i\). For \(j < i\), because \(j(x,p)=i\) is the smallest index with \(\gcd(x/p, a_j)=1\), we have \(\gcd(x/p, a_j) > 1\). Thus \(x/p \in V_{i-1}\). Moreover, \(x/p > 1\) because if \(x/p = 1\) then \(x = p\), but then \(j(x,p)=1\), contradicting \(i \ge 2\).

Let \(m_x\) be a minimal element of \(V_{i-1}\) dividing \(x/p\). Such an element exists: the set of divisors \(d > 1\) of \(x/p\) that belong to \(V_{i-1}\) is nonempty (it contains \(x/p\)) and finite; choose one minimal with respect to divisibility. This \(m_x\) has no proper divisor in \(V_{i-1}\) (otherwise that divisor would also divide \(x/p\) and be in \(V_{i-1}\), contradicting the minimality of \(m_x\) among divisors of \(x/p\)), so \(m_x\) is a globally minimal element of \(V_{i-1}\).

By Lemma 5, the set of all minimal elements of \(V_{i-1}\) is finite. Since \(S\) is infinite, by the pigeonhole principle there exists an infinite subset \(S' \subseteq S\) and a fixed minimal element \(m^*\) of \(V_{i-1}\) such that \(m^* \mid x/p\) for all \(x \in S'\).

Write \(x = p\,m^*\,t\), where \(t = x/(p m^*) \in \mathbb{N}\). Since \(x\) is squarefree and \(m^*\) divides \(x/p\), the prime factors of \(x\) are partitioned into \(\{p\}\), the prime factors of \(m^*\), and the prime factors of \(t\). Hence \(p\), \(m^*\), and \(t\) are pairwise coprime; in particular \(p \nmid m^*\), \(\gcd(m^*, t)=1\), and \(p \nmid t\).

If \(t = 1\) for infinitely many \(x \in S'\), then \(x = p m^*\) would be constant on an infinite set – impossible because \(S'\) is a set of distinct integers. So we may pass to an infinite subset of \(S'\) and assume \(t > 1\) for all \(x \in S'\).

Now take any \(x \in S'\) and any prime \(r \mid t\). Consider \(x/r = p\,m^*\,(t/r)\). We examine \(\gcd(x/r, a_j)\) for \(j \le i\).

- For \(j < i\): Since \(m^* \in V_{i-1}\), we have \(\gcd(m^*, a_j) > 1\). Because \(m^* \mid x/r\), we get \(\gcd(x/r, a_j) \ge \gcd(m^*, a_j) > 1\).
- For \(j = i\): We know \(p \mid a_i\) (Property 2 applied to \(x\), since \(j(x,p)=i\)). Also \(p \mid x/r\). Thus \(\gcd(x/r, a_i) \ge p > 1\).

Therefore, \(\gcd(x/r, a_j) > 1\) for all \(j \le i\). This means that the smallest index \(n\) with \(\gcd(x/r, a_n)=1\) is \(> i\). In particular, \(j(x,r) > i\).

But by condition (d), since \(r \mid x\) and \(r \neq p\) (because \(p \nmid t\)), we have \(j(x,r) < i\). This is a contradiction. ∎

### 7. Finiteness of \(M\)

Assume, for contradiction, that \(M\) is infinite. By Lemma 4, any \(m \in M\) with \(i(m)=1\) is a prime dividing \(a_1\). Since \(a_1\) has finitely many prime divisors, the set \(M_1 = \{\, m \in M \mid i(m)=1 \,\}\) is finite. Thus \(M_2 = \{\, m \in M \mid i(m) \ge 2 \,\}\) is infinite.

We will construct by induction an infinite sequence of infinite sets \(S_0, S_1, S_2, \dots\) and functions \(f_r: S_r \to S_{r+1}\) (\(r \ge 0\)) with the following properties for all \(r \ge 0\) and all \(x \in S_r\):
(i) \(x\) is a minimal element of some \(V_{K_x-1}\) (\(K_x \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}\)).
(ii) \(i_r(x) := i(x)\) (the maximum witness of \(x\) with respect to its \(V_{K_x-1}\)) satisfies \(i_r(x) \ge 2\).
(iii) \(f_r(x)\) is a minimal element of \(V_{i_r(x)-1}\) dividing \(x/p_r(x)\), where \(p_r(x) = p(x)\) is the smallest prime achieving the maximum witness for \(x\).
(iv) If we let \(y = f_r(x)\), then \(i_{r+1}(y) := i(y)\) (computed with respect to \(V_{i_r(x)-1}\)) satisfies \(i_{r+1}(y) \le i_r(x) - 1\) and \(i_{r+1}(y) \ge 2\).
(v) \(f_r(S_r) = S_{r+1}\) (so \(f_r\) is surjective onto \(S_{r+1}\)).

**Base step (\(r=0\)).** Set \(S_0 = M_2\). For each \(x \in S_0\), \(x\) is a minimal element of \(V\) (so \(K_x = \infty\)). We have \(i_0(x) = i(x) \ge 2\), \(p_0(x) = p(x)\). Define \(f_0(x)\) as a minimal element of \(V_{i_0(x)-1}\) dividing \(x/p_0(x)\). Such a minimal element exists because by Property 5 (applied to \(x\) as a minimal element of \(V\) with \(i(x)=i_0(x) \ge 2\)), we have \(x/p_0(x) \in V_{i_0(x)-1}\) and \(x/p_0(x) > 1\); we can then choose a divisor of \(x/p_0(x)\) that lies in \(V_{i_0(x)-1}\) and is minimal with respect to divisibility – this divisor is a globally minimal element of \(V_{i_0(x)-1}\). Let \(T_1 = f_0(S_0)\).

*Case 1: \(T_1\) is finite.* Then there exists \(y \in T_1\) with infinite preimage \(P = f_0^{-1}(y) \subseteq S_0\). For all \(x \in P\), \(f_0(x) = y\). We show that \(i_0(x)\) is constant on \(P\). Since \(y\) divides \(x/p_0(x)\) and \(\gcd(x/p_0(x), a_{i_0(x)}) = 1\) (because \(j(x, p_0(x)) = i_0(x)\)), we have \(\gcd(y, a_{i_0(x)}) = 1\) (any common divisor of \(y\) and \(a_{i_0(x)}\) would divide \(x/p_0(x)\) and \(a_{i_0(x)}\), hence divide their gcd which is \(1\)). Also, \(y \in V_{i_0(x)-1}\) (by definition of \(f_0\)), so \(\gcd(y, a_j) > 1\) for all \(j < i_0(x)\). Therefore, \(i_0(x)\) is the smallest index where \(\gcd(y, a_j) = 1\), which depends only on \(y\). Hence \(i_0(x) = i\) is constant on \(P\).

Also, \(p_0(x) \mid a_i\) (Property 2). Since \(a_i\) has finitely many prime divisors, by the pigeonhole principle there is an infinite subset \(P' \subseteq P\) with the same \(p_0(x) = p\).

Now we verify that \(P'\) satisfies the hypotheses of the Key Lemma (Lemma 6):
- Each \(x \in P'\) is a minimal element of \(V\) (\(K_x = \infty\)) and \(x \in V_i\) (Property 6).
- \(p \mid x\) for all \(x \in P'\).
- \(j(x,p) = i\) for all \(x \in P'\) (since \(p_0(x)=p\) achieves the maximum \(i_0(x)=i\)).
- For any \(q\mid x\), \(q\neq p\), we have \(j(x,q) < i\) (Property 3).
Thus \(P'\) satisfies the Key Lemma, a contradiction.

*Case 2: \(T_1\) is infinite.* For each \(y \in T_1\), \(y = f_0(x)\) for some \(x \in S_0\). As argued above, \(i_0(x)\) is uniquely determined by \(y\); denote it by \(I(y)\). Then \(y\) is a minimal element of \(V_{I(y)-1}\) (by definition of \(f_0\)). Define \(i_1(y)\) as the maximum witness of \(y\) with respect to \(V_{I(y)-1}\). By Property 0 (since \(I(y) = i_0(x) \ge 2\) is finite), we have \(i_1(y) \le I(y)-1 = i_0(x)-1\).

If \(i_1(y) = 1\), then by Lemma 4 (applied to \(y\) as a minimal element of \(V_{I(y)-1}\) with \(I(y) \ge 2\)), \(y\) is a prime dividing \(a_1\). Thus the set of \(y \in T_1\) with \(i_1(y) = 1\) is finite (subset of primes dividing \(a_1\)). Since \(T_1\) is infinite, the set \(U_1 = \{\, y \in T_1 \mid i_1(y) \ge 2 \,\}\) is infinite.

Set \(S_1 = U_1\). Define \(S_0' = f_0^{-1}(S_1)\). Since \(S_1 \subseteq T_1 = f_0(S_0)\) and \(S_1\) is infinite, \(S_0'\) must be infinite (if it were finite, its image under \(f_0\) would be finite). Restrict \(f_0\) to \(S_0' \to S_1\). Then \(f_0(S_0') = S_1\). Rename \(S_0'\) as \(S_0\). Now we have infinite sets \(S_0, S_1\) and a function \(f_0: S_0 \to S_1\) satisfying properties (i)–(v) for \(r=0\).

**Inductive step.** Assume we have constructed infinite sets \(S_0, S_1, \dots, S_r\) and functions \(f_0: S_0 \to S_1, \dots, f_{r-1}: S_{r-1} \to S_r\) satisfying (i)–(v) for all \(k < r\). We now define \(f_r\) on \(S_r\).

For each \(x \in S_r\), we have \(i_r(x) \ge 2\). Let \(p_r(x)\) be the smallest prime achieving the maximum witness for \(x\). Define \(f_r(x)\) as a minimal element of \(V_{i_r(x)-1}\) dividing \(x/p_r(x)\). Such a minimal element exists because by Property 5 (applied to \(x\) as a minimal element of its \(V_{K_x-1}\) with \(i(x)=i_r(x) \ge 2\)), we have \(x/p_r(x) \in V_{i_r(x)-1}\) and \(x/p_r(x) > 1\). Let \(T_{r+1} = f_r(S_r)\).

*Case 1: \(T_{r+1}\) is finite.* Then there exists \(y \in T_{r+1}\) with infinite preimage \(P = f_r^{-1}(y) \subseteq S_r\). For all \(x \in P\), \(f_r(x) = y\). We show that \(i_r(x)\) is constant on \(P\). Since \(y\) divides \(x/p_r(x)\) and \(\gcd(x/p_r(x), a_{i_r(x)}) = 1\) (because \(j(x, p_r(x)) = i_r(x)\)), we have \(\gcd(y, a_{i_r(x)}) = 1\). Also, \(y \in V_{i_r(x)-1}\) (by definition of \(f_r\)), so \(\gcd(y, a_j) > 1\) for all \(j < i_r(x)\). Therefore, \(i_r(x)\) is the smallest index where \(\gcd(y, a_j) = 1\), which depends only on \(y\). Hence \(i_r(x) = i\) is constant on \(P\).

Also, \(p_r(x) \mid a_i\) (Property 2). Since \(a_i\) has finitely many prime divisors, by the pigeonhole principle there is an infinite subset \(P' \subseteq P\) with the same \(p_r(x) = p\).

Now we verify that \(P'\) satisfies the Key Lemma hypotheses:
- Each \(x \in P'\) is a minimal element of some \(V_{K_x-1}\). For \(r=0\), \(K_x = \infty\). For \(r \ge 1\), since \(x \in S_r\) and by construction \(f_{r-1}(S_{r-1}) = S_r\), there exists \(x' \in S_{r-1}\) such that \(x = f_{r-1}(x')\). Then \(x\) is a minimal element of \(V_{i_{r-1}(x')-1}\). So we can take \(K_x = i_{r-1}(x')\).
- \(x \in V_i\): This follows from Property 6 applied to \(x\) as a minimal element of \(V_{K_x-1}\) with \(i(x) = i_r(x) = i\). We must check that the conditions for Property 6 are met: \(i \ge 2\) holds; for finite \(K_x\) we need \(i \le K_x-1\) to conclude \(\gcd(x, a_i) > 1\) from \(x \in V_{K_x-1}\). We have \(i = i_r(x)\) and \(K_x = i_{r-1}(x')\). By (iv) for \(r-1\), \(i_r(x) \le i_{r-1}(x') - 1 = K_x - 1\). So \(i \le K_x-1\) holds. For \(r=0\), \(K_x = \infty\) and \(\gcd(x, a_i) > 1\) follows directly from \(x \in V\). Thus Property 6 gives \(x \in V_i\).
- \(p \mid x\) for all \(x \in P'\).
- \(j(x,p) = i\) for all \(x \in P'\) (since \(p_r(x)=p\) and \(j(x,p_r(x)) = i_r(x) = i\)).
- For any \(q\mid x\), \(q\neq p\), \(j(x,q) < i\) (Property 3).
Thus \(P'\) satisfies the Key Lemma, a contradiction.

*Case 2: \(T_{r+1}\) is infinite.* For each \(y \in T_{r+1}\), \(y = f_r(x)\) for some \(x \in S_r\). As before, \(i_r(x)\) is uniquely determined by \(y\); denote it by \(I(y)\). Then \(y\) is a minimal element of \(V_{I(y)-1}\) (by definition of \(f_r\)). Define \(i_{r+1}(y)\) as the maximum witness of \(y\) with respect to \(V_{I(y)-1}\). By Property 0 (since \(I(y) = i_r(x) \ge 2\) is finite), we have \(i_{r+1}(y) \le I(y)-1 = i_r(x)-1\).

If \(i_{r+1}(y) = 1\), then by Lemma 4 (since \(I(y) \ge 2\)), \(y\) is a prime dividing \(a_1\). Thus the set of \(y \in T_{r+1}\) with \(i_{r+1}(y) = 1\) is finite. Since \(T_{r+1}\) is infinite, the set \(U_{r+1} = \{\, y \in T_{r+1} \mid i_{r+1}(y) \ge 2 \,\}\) is infinite.

Set \(S_{r+1} = U_{r+1}\). Now we perform a backward adjustment to maintain the surjectivity of the functions:
- Let \(S_r' = f_r^{-1}(S_{r+1})\). Since \(S_{r+1} \subseteq T_{r+1} = f_r(S_r)\) and \(S_{r+1}\) is infinite, \(S_r'\) is infinite. Restrict \(f_r\) to \(S_r' \to S_{r+1}\). Then \(f_r(S_r') = S_{r+1}\).
- For \(k = r-1\) down to \(0\): Let \(S_k' = f_k^{-1}(S_{k+1}')\). Since by the induction hypothesis \(f_k(S_k) = S_{k+1}\) (the old \(S_{k+1}\)) and \(S_{k+1}' \subseteq S_{k+1}\), we have \(S_{k+1}' \subseteq f_k(S_k)\). Since \(S_{k+1}'\) is infinite, \(S_k'\) is infinite (otherwise its image would be finite). Restrict \(f_k\) to \(S_k' \to S_{k+1}'\). Then \(f_k(S_k') = S_{k+1}'\).

After this backward adjustment, we have new infinite sets \(S_0', S_1', \dots, S_r', S_{r+1}\) and functions \(f_k: S_k' \to S_{k+1}'\) for \(k=0,\dots,r\) satisfying properties (i)–(v). Rename them as \(S_0, \dots, S_{r+1}\) and continue the induction.

If this construction continues indefinitely, we obtain an infinite sequence of infinite sets \(S_0, S_1, S_2, \dots\) and functions \(f_r: S_r \to S_{r+1}\) with \(i_{r+1}(f_r(x)) \le i_r(x) - 1\) and \(i_r(x) \ge 2\) for all \(x \in S_r\). Pick any \(x_0 \in S_0\) and define \(x_{r+1} = f_r(x_r)\) for \(r \ge 0\). Then \(x_r \in S_r\) and
\[
i_0(x_0) > i_1(x_1) > i_2(x_2) > \cdots \ge 2,
\]
an infinite strictly decreasing sequence of positive integers, which is impossible.

Therefore, the construction must terminate at some finite step with \(T_{r+1}\) finite, yielding a contradiction. Hence our assumption that \(M\) is infinite is false. So \(M\) is finite.

### 8. Periodicity of \(V\)

Since \(M\) is finite and non‑empty, let \(L = \operatorname{lcm}(M)\). For any \(x > 1\), by Corollary 2, \(x \in V \iff \exists\, m \in M,\; m \mid x\). Define
\[
R = \{\, r \in \{0,1,\dots,L-1\} \mid \exists\, m \in M,\; m \mid r \,\}.
\]
(Note that \(0 \in R\) because every \(m \in M\) divides \(0\).) Then
\[
x \in V \iff x \bmod L \in R.
\]
*Proof.* If \(x \in V\), then \(m \mid x\) for some \(m \in M\). Let \(r = x \bmod L\). Since \(m \mid x\) and \(m \mid L\), we have \(m \mid r\), so \(r \in R\). Conversely, if \(r = x \bmod L \in R\), then there exists \(m \in M\) such that \(m \mid r\). Since \(m \mid L\), we have \(m \mid x\), so \(x \in V\). ∎

This equivalence shows that \(V\) is periodic with period \(L\): for all \(x > 1\), \(x \in V \iff x+L \in V\).

### 9. The sequence satisfies \(a_{n+T} = a_n + L\)

Let \(T = |R|\). Since \(a_1 \in V\), we have \(a_1 \bmod L \in R\), so \(T \ge 1\).

We prove by induction on \(n\) that for every \(n \ge 1\),
\[
V \cap [a_n, a_n+L) = \{\, a_n, a_{n+1}, \dots, a_{n+T-1} \,\} \quad \text{and} \quad a_{n+T} = a_n + L.
\]

**Base case \(n=1\).** The interval \([a_1, a_1+L)\) contains exactly one integer from each residue class modulo \(L\). (The integers in this interval are \(a_1, a_1+1, \dots, a_1+L-1\); their residues modulo \(L\) are all distinct and cover all residues \(0,1,\dots,L-1\) exactly once.) The elements of \(V\) in this interval are exactly those with residue in \(R\), so there are exactly \(T\) such elements. Since \((a_n)\) enumerates \(V \cap [a_1, \infty)\) in increasing order (Corollary 1), and all elements of \(V\) in \([a_1, a_1+L)\) are \(< a_1+L\) while any element of \(V \ge a_1+L\) is \(\ge a_1+L\), these \(T\) elements must be the \(T\) smallest elements of \(V \cap [a_1, \infty)\), i.e., \(a_1, a_2, \dots, a_T\). The next element of \(V\) is the smallest element of \(V\) greater than \(a_T\). By periodicity, \(a_1+L \in V\). Since \(a_T < a_1+L\) (because \(a_T \in [a_1, a_1+L)\)) and there are no other elements of \(V\) between \(a_T\) and \(a_1+L\) (any such element would lie in \([a_1, a_1+L)\) and be \(> a_T\), but we already listed all \(T\) elements), we must have \(a_{T+1} = a_1+L\).

**Inductive step.** Assume the statement holds for some \(n \ge 1\). Then
\[
V \cap [a_n, a_n+L) = \{\, a_n, a_{n+1}, \dots, a_{n+T-1} \,\}, \qquad a_{n+T} = a_n+L.
\]
By periodicity,
\[
V \cap [a_n+L, a_n+2L) = \{\, a_n+L, a_{n+1}+L, \dots, a_{n+T-1}+L \,\}
= \{\, a_{n+T}, a_{n+1}+L, \dots, a_{n+T-1}+L \,\}.
\]
Hence
\[
V \cap [a_n, a_n+2L) = \{\, a_n, \dots, a_{n+T-1}, a_{n+T}, a_{n+1}+L, \dots, a_{n+T-1}+L \,\}.
\]

Now consider the interval \([a_{n+1}, a_{n+1}+L)\). From the induction hypothesis we have \(a_n < a_{n+1} < a_n+L\) (since \(a_{n+1} \in [a_n, a_n+L)\) and \(a_{n+1} > a_n\)). Therefore \(a_{n+1}+L < a_n+2L\), so \([a_{n+1}, a_{n+1}+L) \subseteq [a_n, a_n+2L)\). The elements of \(V\) in this interval are those from the above union that lie in \([a_{n+1}, a_{n+1}+L)\):
- \(a_n \notin [a_{n+1}, a_{n+1}+L)\) because \(a_n < a_{n+1}\).
- \(a_{n+1}, a_{n+2}, \dots, a_{n+T-1}\) are all \(\ge a_{n+1}\) and \(< a_n+L\). Since \(a_n+L = a_{n+T} < a_{n+1}+L\) (because \(a_n < a_{n+1}\)), they are all \(< a_{n+1}+L\). Hence they belong to the interval.
- \(a_{n+T} = a_n+L\) satisfies \(a_{n+1} < a_n+L < a_{n+1}+L\) (since \(a_{n+1} < a_n+L\) and \(a_n < a_{n+1}\)), so it belongs.
- \(a_{n+1}+L\) is the right endpoint of the interval, so it is not included.
- \(a_{n+2}+L, \dots, a_{n+T-1}+L\) are all \(\ge a_{n+1}+L\), so they are not in the interval.

Thus
\[
V \cap [a_{n+1}, a_{n+1}+L) = \{\, a_{n+1}, a_{n+2}, \dots, a_{n+T} \,\},
\]
which contains exactly \(T\) elements.

The next element of \(V\) after \(a_{n+T} = a_n+L\) is the smallest element of \(V\) greater than \(a_n+L\). We examine the set \(V \cap [a_n+L, a_n+2L) = \{\, a_n+L, a_{n+1}+L, \dots, a_{n+T-1}+L \,\}\).
- If \(T \ge 2\), then \(a_{n+1}+L\) is in this set and is the smallest element greater than \(a_n+L\).
- If \(T = 1\), this set is just \(\{a_n+L\}\), so there is no element of \(V\) in \((a_n+L, a_n+2L)\). By periodicity, the next interval \([a_n+2L, a_n+3L)\) contains \(a_n+2L \in V\), and there are no elements of \(V\) in \((a_n+L, a_n+2L)\). Hence the smallest element greater than \(a_n+L\) is \(a_n+2L = a_{n+1}+L\).

In both cases, the next element is \(a_{n+1}+L\). Therefore \(a_{n+T+1} = a_{n+1}+L\).

This completes the induction. Consequently, for all \(n \ge 1\),
\[
a_{n+T} = a_n + L.
\]

∎
